la:verb:conicio.gloss: to throw or bring together, unite, connect
senses: to throw or bring together, unite, connect
to throw, drive, force, hurl something
la:verb:conicio.html:
cōnĭcĭo (also conjĭcio and cōicio; cf. Munro ad ; Laber. ap. ), jēci, jectum, 3, v. a. (arch.
temp. perf. conjexi, ) [jacio].
To throw or bring together, to unite, = cogo, colligo.
Lit. (very rare): cum semina rerum coaluerint quae, conjecta repente, etc.,; cf. : palliolum in collum,; (cf. : collecto pallio): sarcinas in medium, Weissenb. (MSS. in medio); ib. § 13; 31, 27, 7: tecta, quae conjectis celeriter stramentis erant inaedificata, Auct. B. G. 8, 5. —
Trop.
To throw together in speaking, to dispute, contend, discuss, manage judicially (ante-class.): verba inter sese, to bandy words, Afran. ap. ; so without verba: noli, mea mater, me praesente cum patre, conicere, p. 267, 30; p. 268, 3: causam conicere hodie ad te volo (conicere, agere, Non.), p. 267, 32; cf. the law formula: ante meridiem causam coiciunto, Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. ; and .—
Like the Gr. συμβάλλειν (v. Lidd. and Scott in h. v. III. 2.), to put together logically, connect, unite; hence (causa pro effectu), to draw a conclusion from collected particulars, to conclude, infer, conjecture (not in Quint., who very freq. employed the synon. colligo): aliquid ex aliquā re,; ; ; : annos sexaginta natus es aut plus, ut conicio,: quid illud mali est? nequeo satis mirari, neque conicere,: cito conjeci, Lanuvii te fuisse,: de futuris,: quam multos esse oporteret, ex ipso navigio,: conicito, possisne necne, etc.,: tu conicito cetera, Quid ego ex hac inopiā capiam,.—
In partic., t. t. of the lang. of augury, to prophesy, foretell, divine from omens, signs (a dream, oracle, etc.); to interpret an omen, a dream, an oracle, etc.: somnium huic,: qui de matre suaviandā ex oraculo Apollinis tam acute arguteque conjecerit,: male conjecta maleque interpretata falsa sunt, etc.,; cf. : num igitur quae tempestas impendeat vatis melius coniciet quam gubernator? etc.,: bene qui coniciet, vatem hunc perhibebo optumum (transl. of a Greek verse),; cf. conjectura, II., conjector, and conjectrix.—
To throw, cast, urge, drive, hurl, put, place, etc., a person or thing with force, quickly, etc., to or towards; and conicere se, to betake, cast, or throw one's self hastily or in flight somewhere (very freq. and class. in prose and poetry).
Lit.
With in: tela in nostros,; ; : pila in hostes,: aliquem in carcerem, ; ; : in vincula,; ; ; ; ; , and et saep.: in catenas,; : in compedes,: in custodiam,; Gai ; : incolas vivos constrictosque in flammam, Auct. B. Afr. 87; cf.: te in ignem,: in eculeum,: hostem in fugam,: exercitum in angustias,: navem in portum (vis tempestatis),: serpentes vivas in vasa fictilia,: cultros in guttura velleris atri,to thrust into,; cf.: ferrum in guttura,: se in signa manipulosque,: se in paludem,: se in sacrarium,: se in ultimam provinciam Tarsum usque,: se in fugam,; so, se in pedes,to take to one's heels, (cf.: se conferre in pedes, Enn. ap. , and ; and: quin, pedes, vos in curriculum conicitis?): se intro,; .—
With dat. (rare): alii spolia ... Coniciunt igni,: huic dea unum anguem Conicit,: facem juveni conjecit,: conjectaque vincula collo accipit,thrown about the neck,.—
With ad: animus domicilia mutet ad alias animalium formas conjectus,removed, transposed,.—
With acc. alone (mostly poet.): magnus decursus aquaï Fragmina coniciens silvarum arbustaque tota,bearing down, prostrating,: jaculum,: tela,: cultros,: thyrsos,: venabula manibus,: domus inflammata conjectis ignibus,: telum inbelle sine ictu,.—(ε) With inter: jaculum inter ilia,.—
Trop., to bring, direct, turn, throw, urge, drive, force something eagerly, quickly to or towards, etc.
With in: aliquem in morbum ex aegritudine,: aliquem in laetitiam,: (hostes) in terrorem ac tumultum,: in metum,: in periculum,: rem publicam in perturbationes,: aliquem in nuptias,; cf. ; 4, 1, 43: (Catilinam) ex occultis insidiis in apertum latrocinium,: aliquem in tricas,; : se in saginam ad regem aliquem,: se mirificam in latebram, to fly to (in disputing), : se in noctem,to commit one's self to the night, travel by night,: se mente ac voluntate in versum, to devote or apply one's self with zeal to the art of poetry, : oculos in aliquem,; ; : orationem tam improbe in clarissimos viros,: tantam pecuniam in propylaea,to throw away, squander,; cf.: cum sestertium milies in culinam conjecisset (Apicius),: culpam in unum vigilem,: crimina in tuam nimiam diligentiam,: maledicta in ejus vitam,: causas tenues simultatum in gregem locupletium, i. e. to cause, occasion, Auct. B. Alex. 49: crimen in quae tempora,: omen in illam provinciam,.—
Absol.: oculos,: petitiones ita conjectae (the fig. taken from aiming at a thing with weapons),: in disputando conjecit illam vocem Cn. Pompeius, omnes oportere senatui dicto audientes esse, threw out or let fall, etc., Cael. ap. .—*
With sub: id vos sub legis superbissimae vincula conicitis,.—
Of a verbal bringing forward, etc., to urge, press, treat, adduce: rem ubi paciscuntur, in comitio aut in foro causam coiciunto, XII. Tab. ap. : causam coicere ad te volo, Afran. ap. (Com. Rel. v. 216 Rib.): verba inter se acrius, p. 267, 27 (Com. Rel. v. 309 ib.): is cum filio Cojecerat nescio quid de ratiunculā, id. ap. (Com. Rel. v. 191 ib.).—
To throw, place, put into, include in, etc.: eum fasciculum, quo illam (epistulam) conjeceram, : ex illo libello, qui in epistulam conjectus est,: conjeci id (prooemium) in eum librum, quem tibi misi,: pluraque praeterea in eandem epistulam conjeci,; cf.: quod multos dies epistulam in manibus habui... ideo multa conjecta sunt aliud alio tempore,: legem in decimam tabulam,; .

senses: a crowding, connecting or uniting together

la:verb:coniveo.gloss: to close or screw up the eyes, blink, wink
senses: to close or screw up the eyes, blink, wink
to overlook, connive or turn a blind eye
la:verb:coniveo.html:
cō-nīvĕo (less correctly con-nī-vĕo; cf. Ritschl, Opusc. II. 448 sq.), nīvi (Cassius ap. P.; cf. Prob. II. p. 1482 ib.) or nixi (Turp. ap. P.;
perh. also connipsi, connipseram, Hildebr. Min.), 2 (access. form of inf. conivĕre, Calvus ap. Prisc. l. l.), v. n.
niveo, kindr. with nico and nicto
, to close or shut. *
In gen.: cava ventris ac stomachi inanitate diutinā contrahuntur et conivent,.—More freq.,
Esp., to close or shut the eyes (in sleep, from the light, from fear, etc.), to blink; or of the eyes, to close, shut, to half close when heavy with sleep (class. in prose and poetry).
Lit.: dum ego conixi somno, hic sibi prospexit vigilans virginem, Turp. l. l.; so ; : coniventes illi oculi abavi tui,: conivent solemque pavent agnoscere visu,; cf. : ad tonitrua et fulgura,: contra conminationem aliquam (gladiatores),.—With acc. Gr.: nam non conivi oculos ego deinde sopore, Cassius, l. l.: (oculis) somno coniventibus,; .—*
Poet., transf., of the sun and moon, to be darkened, obscured, eclipsed, .—
Trop.
In gen., to be dull, drowsy, or languid: certa sunt enim pleraque et nisi coniveamus, in oculos incurrunt,: multa nobis blandimenta natura ipsa genuit, quibus sopita virtus coniveret,: animus atque mens viri prudentis in sollicitis numquam conivens, nusquam aciem suam flectens, etc.,; cf. .—
(Like our phrase to wink at.) To leave an error or crime unnoticed or uncensured, to overlook, connive at, wink at, etc.: haec ipsa concedo: quibusdam etiam in rebus coniveo,: pro di immortales! cur interdum in hominum sceleribus maxumis aut conivetis aut ... poenas in diem reservetis?: qui ob eam causam in tot tantisque sceleribus conivebant,; ; Fragm. ap. Prob. II. p. 1482 P.: seditiosorum punitor acerrimus, conivebat in ceteris,; .

la:verb:conitor.html:
cō-nītor (less correctly con-nītor; cf.
Ritschl, Opusc. II. 448 sq.), nisus or nix us (conisus,; ; et saep.; ; Ser. Ep. 94, 31; ; ; ; : conixus, B. and K.; ; ; ; et saep.; ; ; ; ; ), 3, v. dep. (inf. conitier, Att. ap. ; cf. Trag. Rel. p. 284 Rib.), to put forth all one's strength, strive, struggle, endeavor.
Lit., of physical exertion.
In gen.
Absol. or with abl. of means: pol si quidem Conisus esses, per corium, per viscera Perque os elephanti transmineret bracchium,: dein ejus germanum cornibus conitier, Att. ap. (Trag. Praet. v. 23 Rib.): corniger est valido conixus corpore taurus,; cf.: atque genu flexo Taurus conititur ingens, (536): illam famuli ferebant, conixi umeris,: dextrā,: fert ingens toto conixus corpore saxum,: adversis Conixi incurrunt hastis,: undique omnes conisi hostem avertunt,; : omnibus copiis conisus Ancus,: tres juvenes conixi arborem unam evellebant,; : Antiochus omnibus regni viribus conixus,: ni equestre proelium conixi omni vi perficerent,: totis conisus viribus,: si coniterentur (mulae),.—
With inf.: coniterentur modo uno animo omnes invadere hostem, Weissenb. ad loc.: inligare conisa est,; .—
With ut: (parvi) conituntur sese ut erigant,.—
With ad and acc.: ut rursus ad surgendum coniti non possent,: ceteris ad convincendum eum conisis,: omnibus imperii nervis ad revocandam pristinae disciplinam militiae conisus est,.—
Esp.,
To press upon, press toward, struggle toward, strive to reach; with in and acc. of place: equitatus summum in jugum virtute conititur,: in unum locum,: praealtam in arborem,.—So poet., of a weapon: in hastam,.—Of things: in quem coepere locum conixa feruntur (primordia rerum),.—
To struggle in giving birth, to labor (cf. enitor): spem gregis, ah! silice in nudā conixa reliquit,. —
Trop., of mental effort, etc.: praesto est domina omnium et regina, ratio, quae conixa per se et progressa longius, fit perfecta virtus,putting forth her own energy,: quantum coniti animo potes,.
